utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, at pages 96 through 101, we talked about a document, your prior statement, and you indicated that you used the word "unit" in that document to refer to your battalion and not your company. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, would it surprise you that throughout your testimony yesterday, you used the word "unit" to refer to your company? Would that surprise you? Or do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That throughout your testimony yesterday, sir, you used the word "unit" or you used the phrase "my unit" to refer to your company. Do you recall that? You did that many times, ten or more times yesterday, from the beginning of your testimony to the end.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, for example, on page 11, "the troops along the same axis where my unit, my company, was deployed ..." you're obviously referring to your unit, being your company; isn't that correct? Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you are asserting that I was engaged with my company during combat up to the Danube River or the hotel Dunav. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, when you said this line, "The troops along the same axis where my unit, my company, was deployed," you were obviously using "unit" and "company" interchangeably, weren't you, yesterday, sir? That's page 4 -- I'm sorry, page 11 of the transcript. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May counsel lower his voice? Counsel keeps on speaking and he's within, I'd say, 2 to 3 metres of the defendant, of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It can be disruptive. If you could take care of that, please, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were using those two words interchangeably in that phrase yesterday, on page 11; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that I was clear yesterday, and I stand by my position from yesterday. Right now I cannot be sure about what you're saying, if that's the gist of what I said or not. I really cannot -- you are putting to me that I said something. I have to recall what I said at what point. But I think that I was clear. What I said yesterday is something that I stand by now today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's continue. Let's move to page 19. "At that point in time, I was commanding a unit consisting of professional soldiers, soldiers who had contracts with the Army of Yugoslavia, professional service contracts." Again, sir, you're referring to your company, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were soldiers who, in 1992, for the first time, at least to my knowledge, had signed a professional contract, as professional soldiers under contract. And at the time, in my company, there were about 60 soldiers, meaning --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, again, the question is: You were referring to company -- your company when you used the word "unit" in that particular phrase.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 39, you were asked: "Did you at any time during combat operations send a report to Sljivancanin about combat operations?" And you responded, in answer, on page 39: "When visiting my unit, I was obliged to inform Mr. Sljivancanin with the current situation, to inform him about what I knew in relation to information that he sought." Again, you're referring to your unit as your company in that situation, when he visited your company; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. Are you trying to tell me that I made a mistake or that I'm referring to my company as "unit"? Yes, I used the term "unit" when I meant my company, when I meant my battalion, when I meant my brigade. I don't see what the mistake is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you continually used the word "unit" yesterday to refer to your company; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaning my company, battalion and brigade, depending on who I was referring to at that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you continually used the word "unit" yesterday to refer to your company. Let's continue. Page 57, you're speaking about having secured the hospital. "My unit was then withdrawn from this assignment, and we took no further steps within the hospital compound or in the hospital building itself, not myself, not my unit." Again, you were referring to members of your company when you used the word "unit"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 72: "Then, now, and always I would say that pertaining to the assignment being carried out by my unit, that is also my personal assignment ..." Again, you're referring to your unit's personal assignment as your company's assignment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably you are correct on this point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And later on that same page, you say: "So when it says here in the text 'following the handover of the security of the hospital compound I withdrew my unit to the previous location,' it means that that was my assignment and I was obliged to implement it." Again, you're referring to your unit as your company.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Part of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then move on to page 94: "A company is assigned its axis of action, and this is the lowest unit of permanent composition." Again, you're referring to your company and your unit interchangeably in that phrase, aren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, the only time that you referred to your unit as a battalion was in an attempt to change your testimony yesterday, to come up with an excuse for why you previously indicated that your unit was in combat to November 17th; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Would you allow me to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the record speaks for itself. It's obvious. You were using that to change your previous statement. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that before we finish. Let's try and get some other subjects covered. You testified yesterday that you were not at your residence or, if you want to call, your place of sleeping or residence/observation post on the evening, or sometime during the latter part of the evening, of November 20th. You testified to that at pages 2 through 5, that you went to a roasted pig dinner. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some meat. There was probably other kinds of meat, too, but I think there was also pork.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you don't have any writings, diary or calendar, to support that or to corroborate that, do you, at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't note down such things, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And this dinner was in Petrova Gora, and that's the same section of where your residence/observation post is located, also in the Petrova Gora section; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that it was about a kilometre and a half from the place where I was sleeping, or perhaps 2 kilometres. I slept in Nova Ulica street and the observation post of Lieutenant Vuckovic was in Oslobodjenje street, which was towards the exit from Vukovar. But it's all part of Petrova Gora. That's at least how we understood it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And by vehicle, how far of a drive is it? Five minutes, ten minutes at the most?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very short drive. A couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, even though Witnesses P22 and P18 claim that they saw you at your lodging or observation post, you deny that you were there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that neither of the two were at the observation post that evening, but they slept at the place where all of these soldiers were billeted, where all of the soldiers were sleeping. That's what I assert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So basically you're asserting that you could not have talked to them and learned of the murders that night because you weren't there; isn't that basically your claim?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that the way in which each one described the event was actually not the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: Are you basically claiming that, since you weren't at that observation post, you weren't able to speak with them that evening and learn of the murders? Is that basically the gist of your claim?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that some of the Belgrade accused denied committing murders at Ovcara, since, like you, they were also at a dinner on the evening of November 20th, 1991? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard that story, but I think that we heard here in this courtroom from Witness P022 who made up what and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that these people claim to be having dinner with you that night; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you are aware, as you just said, that P022 indicated that this dinner alibi was all manufactured to avoid liability for the murders at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They talked about another dinner altogether allegedly at a place belonging to a woman in Nova street, and that has absolutely nothing to do with the place where I was. I said that the place is about 2 kilometres away. As for Witness P022, that witness stated here that the story was manufactured in the circle of people that he communicated with. As far as I recall, Mr. Borovic put questions to him relating to that dinner and he answered those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know, sir, just as that was manufactured, that the court in Belgrade rejected that so-called dinner alibi and convicted those accused. You're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I put to you, sir, just like they manufactured that alibi, your alibi, your dinner alibi, is also manufactured to avoid liability.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true. And I would ask you to present any kind of evidence that would corroborate what you are asserting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you have no documentary evidence to support your claim, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that you will find any officer writing in his work diary, "I am going to dinner." That is not the sort of information that would be recorded in a work diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: You have no documentary evidence of any kind supporting your dinner alibi, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But there are people, live people, who were with me there, and I hope that they will appear before this Trial Chamber and you and will tell their story.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Friends of yours; correct? Friends and former associates.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you think that all friends are prepared to lie and provide an alibi just so that they could save somebody? Of course, some of them are my friends, some are my acquaintances, but that is absolutely not a reason for them to lie or do anything wrong in order to help me. If you would allow me a short digression, I am sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But we know, sir, that witnesses and accused did that and lied in the Belgrade court in relation to the Ovcara murders. We know that did, in fact, occur, and you know that, too.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do not place me in the same basket with the accused in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try and cover a few more subjects quickly. You testified on Monday that each night you prepared plans for the next day's operations for the assault group, and that's at page 12621. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, since now I understand the importance of using the proper term: I did not conduct operations, I was conducting tactical actions. Operations are conducted by corps and operations groups, so I was not at that level. Now I can answer your question. Unless a cease-fire was ordered, one that was agreed between the two sides at higher levels, in such cases, I did not plan anything. If, the next day, there was an action being carried out in which my company also took part, or the assault group, then I would plan the communications system and the manner of the unit's actions. I repeat once again: I did all of this until the fall of Milovo Brdo. After that - I give you my word - I did not draft a single letter on the map or issue any commands to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified that you gave them the tasks in the morning - and that's at 12621 - just before their actions.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders of the squads or groups were given these instructions, if there were such, so that I could monitor their implementation of the tasks. This was done so that I could have an overview of the situation at any given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "tasks" and "instructions," you're referring to orders; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. See, we all received combat orders from our commanders, and on the basis of that combat order, we would make an evaluation or assessment of our assignments. That is how I also assessed my assignments. And then, in the spirit of carrying out that assignment, I would specifically set the tasks for each group or squad. I already had my assignment. We all had our assignment. But then we would translate that into actions on the ground. The battalion commander didn't tell me, "This squad should go here, this squad should go there," and so on. No. This was something that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if you received the orders from the battalion commander, you issued those orders to the commander of the -- the commanders of the assault group; isn't that correct? For example, if they told you the time to go into action, you would then issue the orders with the plan that you drafted; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to correct one thing. During the period, as I described it, after the 20th of October until the 10th of November, there was only one assault group, not several assault groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question was: After you received, for example, the time from the battalion to go into action, you issued those orders with your plan to the commanders of the assault group; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive the information. The battalion commander doesn't give information; he issues orders. I would then relay his orders to a lower level and then implement it on the ground. That would be a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, on page 12621, you stated: [As read] "Since I used to draw up such plans before any action, for reasons of security, I would do that immediately prior, prior to action. I never drew up a plan and set it aside for the next two days or so but I always do it the night before. Since we coordinated, and since the battalion commander would tell us the exact time when we were to go into action at the level of battalion and the brigade, I always issued those orders to those commanders which were part of the assault group immediately prior to going into action, that is the morning, that is that morning. If we were to start attacking at 7 a.m., if we were all assembled at 6.30, I used to issue those tasks, 10 minutes to 15 -- 10 to 15 minutes before we were supposed to set out." Do you agree with that, sir? Do you agree with your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With most of it, but I insist that it's either a question of interpretation or in terms of marking my statement, one thing should be changed: There aren't any commanders in the sense of komandant. The lowest level unit where there is a komandant commander is a battalion, whereas platoons, companies, assault groups, squads, have commanders in the sense of komandir. So, in the doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army, they are not commanders in the sense of komandant, and that is a crucial difference in terms of command and control. So there are no komandants of assault groups, companies, platoons, and squads. As for the rest, all of it is correct. That is exactly what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you know that, according to JNA rules and regulations, even you as a komandir as opposed to a komandant, as a komandir, you can issue orders to your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So whether you're a komandir or a komandant, you can still issue orders to your subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I "can". It is my duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you testified that you were the one who drew up these plans, since you were the only person of that group who had attended military academy, since the leaders of the TOs or the Leva Supoderica unit, they hadn't attended military academy and they weren't professional soldiers like you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you coordinated -- you testified that you coordinated the actions along -- or their actions along your axis, and you had to coordinate them, I'd suggest to you, because there were several people involved in various tasks on that axis.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the task that I was given by my battalion commander, and I carried it out as best I could and as best I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that since several people were involved in an action, large numbers of men, and you coordinated their action, that that's why, sir, the soldiers of the Vukovar TO and the Leva Supoderica unit were placed under your command. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just want to say the following as well: I coordinated with the battalion from the reserve force that came from Kragujevac. I also coordinated with the TO detachment that had come from the village of Berak next to Vukovar. I also coordinated with some other units that were along that axis, but I did not command those units. They had their own superiors. I just said, "This is your assignment," and I took care that they would carry out that assignment as best they could and should. Sometimes on that axis, there could be lots of people, a great many people. I didn't count them, but sometimes there would be over a thousand people; that is to say, could I, as a company commander, command over 1.000 people? That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you say you coordinated, "coordinated" is one aspect of command. You were controlling those units. When you gave them those tasks, they couldn't say no. You gave them orders.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot accept responsibility for something that I did not have responsibility for. I cannot accept responsibility for that, that I had been issued with an order stating that I was responsible for the life and work and activity of the units that you are suggesting. I could not have done that and I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the assault group lasted until November 17th and that you remained as commander of that assault group until the end of November 17th or 18th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, could you just tell me where you got that information from?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that their activities continued through the 17th and 18th and that actually you remained as commander until you left on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That is a sheer assumption and it is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who Sasa Bojkovski is? He was a fellow company commander of yours. You've mentioned him in your testimony. You know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of the 1st Motorised Company from the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were the commander of the 3rd Motorised Company.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would it surprise you that Sasa Bojkovski has given a statement saying that you were still an assault group commander on November 17th? And he --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A procedural matter. This is the first time that we hear of this statement being put to the witness. We can follow but we haven't got the statement. However, if it doesn't bother the witness or the Trial Chamber, then I'll accept. Then I'm going to present some statements that we had not announced at all and that were not before this Court at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just a statement in relation to this specific incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it part of the discovered documents on the 65 ter list? Has notice been given of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm almost positive. It's an older document. May I have one moment to consult?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll check at the break. It's one of a number of statements, and I was under the impression it was, in fact, disclosed with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment it's subject to objection by Mr. Borovic on the basis that he knows nothing of it, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will withdraw that and check at the break and get some dates. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be continuing until the break, will you, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is there a limit going to be placed on cross-examination today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood last night you were near the end. Is this the effect of reviving overnight?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll see if we can move quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were interviewed on two occasions in 1998 in Belgrade, and never once in either interview did you say that "the Serbian paramilitaries or Serbian troops who committed the crimes were not part of my unit." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. Could you please repeat the question? I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No problem, sir. You were interviewed twice in 1998 in Belgrade, and at any time -- at no time during those interviews did you state that "the Serbian troops or paramilitaries who committed the crimes at Ovcara were not part of my company."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They were not part of my company, my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you never stated that in those statements to Belgrade, either to the court or to the security organs, in either statement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I was answering the questions that were put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you never made that statement, that "the Serbian paramilitaries who committed the crimes were never part of my company." You never said that in Belgrade, in either interview; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You expect me to confirm that. Although I was not at Ovcara, I did not see with my own eyes who committed the crime, you expect me to say that those soldiers who committed that crime were not members of my unit? How can I know who it was that committed the crime if I had not seen that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked about your views of the indictment and that's what is stated in the indictment. So my question is: At no time -- isn't it true that at no time you stated, did you -- I'm sorry, at no time did you state that "the Serbian paramilitaries who committed the crimes were not part of my company." Isn't it true that you never stated that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask you kindly if I could have a look, but I'm sure that you've had a look and that it is not contained in any one of my statements. I kindly ask you not to put me in a position to state something which was absolutely not within my awareness. I absolutely did not know who committed that at that point in time. How can I state something that someone did not belong there? So until this witness, P022, took the stand here, or rather until I got his statement, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked about the indictment and it's stated in those indictments, and you denied what was in the indictment. But you never said, sir, "those Serbian paramilitaries" or you never said, "those locals, the Vukovar TO, the Leva Supoderica unit, those people were not part of my command." You never said that in either interview in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one asked me that at that time. Had somebody asked me that, had somebody put the question to me, of course I would have answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were asked if you had committed the crimes and you were asked about the indictment, and you denied -- made certain denials in relation to the indictment. But you never said that "the soldiers or the local TO, the Leva Supoderica, the volunteers, were not part of my company." Isn't that correct? You never made that statement; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Had somebody asked me about that, I would have told them what I told you just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir -- sir, you're aware, from the Belgrade trial, that Miroljub Vujovic has given a statement both to the court and the investigative judge that he was under your command, that he and his unit were under your command. Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deny -- well, I know that he stated that, but that is his mode of defence. I deny that that is the truth, the way he had put it. But I told you -- well, you heard the testimony of his commander here as well. So I absolutely deny that that is the truth, as Miroljub Vujovic had put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, at the trial in Belgrade, Vujovic defends you, makes no accusations against you and even commends you. Knowing that, will you accept his testimony that you were his commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I remember correctly, I was also praised by Witness P022 and P024 and P018, but that does not mean that I agree with their statements, the statements that they made here, just as I do not agree with the allegations made by Miroljub Vujovic, if he really did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Milan Lancuzanin, known as Kameni, who you've mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute now. Yes, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, although he answered a great many questions here, and I told him not to present his wishes here, but the Trial Chamber decided that these statements that were given by the members of Leva Supoderica to the police cannot be taken into account. Now, what Lancuzanin stated and before what organs, all of that, what was submitted by the Prosecution a minute before Radic started testifying is something that we cannot use and should not use. This is a question of principle. The Prosecutor should not abuse the wish of the accused, because we are in a court of law, after all, and it is for the Court to set the rules and we are to follow them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was under the impression that we were allowed to confront people -- confront a witness with a statement and ask for his opinion based on it and to see if it changes his testimony. I wasn't here throughout trial, so if there might be a rule that I'm unaware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is correct. I think Mr. Borovic is referring to the very recent decision of this Chamber concerning particular statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was under the impression that each defendant can be impeached, if you wanted, with their own particular statement, but that does not concern the statements of other persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statements of other accused may not be put. That is what our -- to a witness which is a decision that we have given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that an accused in this case or other accused in any case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The accused in this case. The particular statements, there were six of them, all in 1998, two by each of the three accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These statements here are not part of any of those particular statements. These are statements that these accused made in the Belgrade court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are they statements of which notice has been given to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, also in that other statement, disclosure was given 19 January 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, I missed the last part of that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to that other statement, the Bojkovski statement that was mentioned, earlier disclosure was given 19 January 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic, for the purpose of testing the credibility of this witness, statements made by others, not the three accused that were the subject of our decision, may be put to them. Normally, it would simply be a matter of an oral question, which is what is being done by Mr. Weiner at the present time. It is, of course, exactly what the Defence did with Prosecution witnesses when any previous statements of those witnesses or of others, given either to this Tribunal or in other proceedings, whether in Belgrade or elsewhere, or to other investigating authorities in the present Serbia or the former Yugoslavia, were used by different Defence counsel, including yourself. It's the same position but in reverse. It's simply calling for this witness to say whether or not that affects his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, everything you said in relation to discovery and putting statements to witnesses by the Prosecution is correct. Those are statements that have to do with witnesses that we heard in this courtroom, whereas what Mr. Weiner is trying to do now has to do with your decision taken a day or two ago; namely, to show witness statements to the witness that we had not received. The last one he tried to put to the witness is one of those five or six statements for which you decided that they cannot be put to the witness a minute or two before they -- the witness before he starts giving evidence. We did not discuss that with the witness, and it is our right to be able to follow what the Prosecutor is putting to the witness. This decision was in force. Again, the Prosecutor is trying to put to this witness some witness statements, and again we are not in a position to follow, because we observed your decision. We do not have these witness statements before us and there is no reason -- I mean, I know what credibility is, and this would be an adventure that Radic would be embarking upon. But it doesn't make sense, from the point of view of procedure, to put something to the accused now that we were not in a position to discuss with him earlier on. And he, as a witness, was not preparing along those lines and had no opportunity to prepare. After all, this is 12 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it has to do specifically with the names my learned friend is putting now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. It seems, Mr. Weiner, this last statement at least is one subject to the objection raised very early on by Mr. Borovic; that there had not been the required notice given that this would be a document used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, the Court indicated that we could not introduce it, that we would not show it, but we could still confront a witness with it. But if the Court wants to change that, I can move on, whatever the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, you accept it is one of the documents affected by that ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. Our position was and is, Mr. Borovic, that the document, not having been given the correct notice, may not be put to the witness as a document, but the witness can be asked whether or not he is aware that a statement to a certain effect has been given, which is different from his evidence. If the source of that proves to be one of the statements, it might be open to you, if you are not in a position to re-examine on it, to seek leave to do some unusual things, such as defer your re-examination about that; even to have leave to take instructions from your client about it before you re-examine him on it. Now, they are very unusual courses. It would be rare that the circumstances would persuade us that they were appropriate, but they can be if the document really is of considerable importance and significance to you. Now, I suspect these may not. They are, perhaps, typical of statements made by a variety of people which say a wide range of things, some of which are different in some detail, some of which contradict the evidence of your client. And your client just will say of such a statement put to him, "That's not correct," or "I don't understand how that could be," or whatever it was, and that is as far as your client can take it. And the Prosecution isn't able to go any further because it has not been part of their case and they haven't given you proper notice about it. They can't set about trying now to prove the truth of that statement. So it's not going to be evidence against your client for its truth. The only evidence will be your client's reaction to hearing that somebody has said something different to his evidence. And I guess there are a very large number of people who might come into that category for right or wrong. Carry on, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that the Leva Supoderica unit was under your command through November 21st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we've had testimony in this court - Witness 024 - that Kameni's unit was under Radic's command, and it had to be so since Kameni wasn't a real commander - and that's Milan Lancuzanin, as you know - because he's not a real commander. Do you deny that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, my personal conviction during the evidence of Witness P024 is that that man was never there at all, that he just talked about certain events. He knows about some facts, but he is not aware of all the events that took place. He said somethings that are ridiculous even to this Honourable Trial Chamber. He says that Major Tesic was commander of the 4th Company, which is ridiculous. But let me go back to the statement itself. It has to do with a comment of one witness who was a soldier, who was at Petrova Gora all the time, according to his own statement, and who absolutely does not know about the system of command and control. If that is his impression, I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to give a qualification of that impression. If it is your assessment that I commanded Leva Supoderica, then I will accept that. But I was never the commander of Leva Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, sir, it was under your command, as was the TO and these other units, all under your assault group, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you allow the witness to react, if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't that true, sir, that it was all under your command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced that you, yourself, do not believe in the truth of this statement. Leva Supoderica was under the command of Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, and Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, went to get his orders from Major Tesic from time to time, orders, instructions, tasks. A part of the Territorial Defence that was under the command of Miroljub Vujovic was under his command. He received his tasks from his commander, as his commander explained here before this Court, and I coordinated the work in the field only during combat, not a second after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Witness 022 has testified that the TO members and the Leva Supoderica unit were under your command for the Vukovar operations. Do you deny that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. Witness 022 was just an ordinary soldier. He is not familiar with the command and control system. He saw that I was participating in the tasks that I myself carried out, that I received from my superior command. He had no idea as to what exactly I was doing. He gave his impression of -- his interpretation of what he saw. But I absolutely deny that what Witness 022 stated is true. I don't think that he is a person that is competent enough to give this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Witness 018 has placed the local Chetniks, which is referring to the Leva Supoderica unit, to being under Radic's command. Do you deny that also?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do deny this. Again, I gave you my opinion of Witness 018. It was a soldier whom I really had to put in my pocket, keep him there to keep him alive. He did not know what his duties were, let alone mine. And if you allow me to go back to Witness P022, when your colleague asked him - I don't recall who conducted the examination but the question was - whether the Territorial Defence and Leva Supoderica were incorporated into my company, he confirmed that this was correct. But when Mr. Borovic asked him what it means, "incorporated," he said, "I don't know." And now you're talking to me about his competence and asking me to accept his statement which, of course, I cannot do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, all these people, some with no personal relationship or association to each other, have all maintained that you were the commander of either/or -- either the Vukovar TO and/or the Leva Supoderica unit during that time in Vukovar. Having heard these people who were not related to each other, will you admit that you were their commander, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that I was the commander of the 3rd Motorised Company and I accept all those things that I have already stated before this Honourable Court. I do not accept the statements made by people who were not part of the command and control system, those who were not familiar with it and those who merely presented their own impressions. Of course, the impressions have nothing to do with the actual truth. I have to apologise, I would really like to have been able to hear my commander here. I was rather hoping he would come here to testify. He would be the competent person to testify about this. But a soldier who volunteered to join the Leva Supoderica unit, for him to give us his views, it is strange. I find it strange, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you subpoenaed the commander, your commander, Major Tesic, to testify? If he's the one who could clarify all this in your favour, have you subpoenaed him to testify? The answer is no; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Borivoje Tesic was on your witness list, Mr. Weiner. Now, why he didn't come here to testify, it was your call. I called my witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Have you subpoenaed him to testify? You just indicated that he's the person who can clarify it all in your favour. Isn't it true you haven't subpoenaed him because he would not testify in your favour; he would testify that those units were under your command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I have gone through the statement made by Major Tesic to the investigative organs, to the OTP investigators, with great care.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, so have I. The question is: Have you subpoenaed him? And you haven't, since he wouldn't testify in your favour; is that correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you didn't call your counterpart, Bojkovski, because he would tell you that you attended an assault group commander meeting on the 17th with the other assault group commanders; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise, but this is a ridiculous statement to make. I really don't want to be mocking anyone, but what you just stated here is just a jumble of facts. What meeting of the assault group? There was no meeting of assault group, least of all on the 17th. I don't know where you get this information from. I have never heard of any such meeting taking place anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At Major Tesic's command post, the evening of November 17th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I will now make a following assertion: The battalion commander, Mr. Tesic, labelled companies as assault groups, and I can now say that the 2nd Company was not a platoon-strength unit, so it could not have been an assault group. So this is a totally wrong term. I am not going to now evaluate the quality of work of my commander. This is for somebody else to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: Isn't it true that you attended, you were one of the assault group commanders who attended a meeting at Major Tesic's office on November 17th, Major Tesic's command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of the 3rd Motorised Company, and I attended a briefing with the battalion commander on the 17th of November, 1991. That is the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On the evening of November 19th, could you tell us where you were on that evening?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, after coming back from the briefing with the battalion commander, I took a bath; I changed my clothes. So I just rested a bit and did something for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you attend another dinner on that evening, too?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've had testimony in this court from Witness 002 that on the morning of November 21st, he was discussing with others and learned of the murders of prisoners inside of your apartment/observation post. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time that I heard about this version of events was when Witness P002 explained it or testified about it. I, myself, have never seen that in this way, this version of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I waited until my client made his answer and now I want to say that Witness P002, in fact this is an assertion made by the Prosecution, and now I would like the Prosecutor to be quite specific. What is it that he actually had in mind, the statement made by the witness or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just as I asked it; that P002 learnt about the murders of prisoners at Ovcara on the morning of November 21st inside of his apartment/observation post, and I asked the witness if he knew anything about that and did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were asked if that is based upon evidence, on a statement or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's based on his testimony at pages 10398 to 10399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness 002 testified that on the morning of November 21st, there was discussion of the murder of prisoners just outside of your apartment/observation post. And that's at 10400 -- page 10400 of the transcript. Do you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know absolutely nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness 002 testified at page 10400 that Stanko Vujanovic was outside of your apartment/observation post complaining that too many people were talking about the murders at Ovcara. Do you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Witness P002 invented the whole thing. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you know that Stanko Vujanovic - and you were staying in his family home or family complex - was the same individual who was convicted for those murders in Ovcara at the court in Belgrade; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know that Stanko Vujanovic's wife, Nada Kalaba, who was staying at your home/observation post, was also convicted for the crimes at Ovcara. You know that, too, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see what that has to do with me. I know that she also was convicted. Does that mean that I am guilty because, from time to time, I would see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, my next question is: Since you were staying at their family compound, did you ever hear from either one of those people what happened in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, as an officer, throughout my life, I tried to be honourable and honest, and I did not allow any arbitrary acts by my superiors -- by my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we have ten minutes. I want to finish at the break -- by the break. Could you just answer the question? Did you hear from Stanko Vujanovic or his wife, Nada Kalaba, about the murders at Ovcara? You can say "yes"; you can say "no"; or "maybe".

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed this with them, or they did not dare to mention that in front of me because they knew very well what my views of that would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There was testimony that a woman by the name of Dragica or Daca was describing the murders in your house and observation post. And that's at page 10398-10399, Witness 002. Did you hear that conversation, sir; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard Witness P022. Dragica is dead and she can neither confirm nor deny this. I, myself, have never heard about this conversation or that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That morning, according to testimony, Dragica was complaining that too many people were talking -- that others were talking too much about the murders. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't ask me about Dragica. I did not see Dragica at all. I think I actually saw her only once, when there was a little bit of confusion, but I never spoke to her at all. I don't know what she was saying, nor was it my duty to know what she was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you never heard anything, with all this discussion happening, you never heard anything; is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my testimony that I was never in a position where discussions were held about any crime. Had I been in such a situation, I can put my life on the line here and say that it would not just go like that, unpunished. I cannot abide anyone being unfairly charged with anything, accused of anything. But to let somebody go unpunished for a crime, that is something that is completely unacceptable to me. This is not the kind of a man and an officer that I was. For me, I take it as an insult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that none of your soldiers told you about the murders that occurred in Ovcara, including your soldiers who participated in that murder -- in those murders?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was committed by my soldiers. I heard what Witness P022 said. Many things in his testimony are not quite clear to me, but sitting here on the witness stand, I have to express my doubts about many things that he said. I don't know, in fact, whether he's a normal person at all, when he was able to say all those things. I'm not trying to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did any of your soldiers tell you about the murders?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, because I would have eaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Eaten up? Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm being metaphorical here. I would not have allowed anyone to go unpunished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Witness P022, who you mentioned, testified that he participated in the murders, he told you about the murders at Ovcara, and on the following day he provided you with an update about those murders. Do you still claim that you were unaware of the murders at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In his first statement, Witness P022, he said himself that I would have killed him had he told me that. I don't know whether I would have killed him, but he would not have gone unpunished. The statement that he made before this Court is ridiculous, and, in fact, it's offensive to me. I find it offensive. And he knows it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness P0118 testified that while he was at your apartment/observation post, they were talking very loudly about the murders and you were sitting not very far away. They were celebrating what they had done. Do you still claim that you were unaware of the murders at Ovcara on November 20th and November 21st?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to correct you here. Witness P018 said that he had been present there while the murders had been discussed, but he did not know about the murders, he was just learning about them. And I say that this situation did not occur as he described it. I'm putting my life on the line here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness 002, who is not a business associate, a military associate, of 018 and 022, has testified that he had a brief discussion with you on November 21st, in the morning, about those murders. Do you still claim that you were unaware of them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your allegation that he was not their associate in any way, I think, is not correct. Witness P022 stated that he had seen Witness P002 in the place where he lived. Why would they see each other? Why a soldier, an ordinary soldier, felt the need to see his commander? I don't know what the relationship was, but there was a relationship. I can say that on November 21st, in the morning, I absolutely did not know of any murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, an error in the transcript. The witness stated why would Witness P022 see a journalist, P002, and the transcript says "commander." That is not what the witness said. He said why would Witness P022 see Witness P002, the commander, and the word "commander" was not mentioned at all by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you know that reporters see lots of people and speak to lots of people to get information for stories, but that doesn't mean that they are associated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I put to you that in that small community of soldiers in Vukovar, there is no way that you could have not known about the murders occurring at Ovcara, and that you, in fact, knew about them and did nothing.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my testimony that there was no such thing as a small community of soldiers the way you are trying to paint it. And it is also my testimony that I would either use the help of the military police or I would do it myself; I would have taken any measure available to bring those people to justice. I would do the same with my brother had he been in such a situation, let alone a witness who is a soldier or anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as promised, finished by the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Weiner. We will resume at 25 minutes past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have a question for Mr. Radic. This will not take long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radic, the Prosecutor asked you about the two statements you provided in 1998. When you gave the first statement in March 1998, and when you were summoned, did you know at all what you were going to talk about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you gave your second statement, did you find out before or after that that you would have the status of a suspect in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in 1998, and through the media, I found out that I was accused before this Tribunal for acts that I did not commit. And when I was summoned to the military court, shortly before my testimony, the president of the military tribunal at the time - I think it was Colonel or General Gojevic - handed me the indictment from this Tribunal, which I received and signed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Since you said that you were imprecise, that you didn't recall dates, when did you get down to remembering, and what did you do in order to know the details, the dates, such as the 18th, the 19th and the 20th? Was this after the trial before the military court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was before I came here to the Hague Tribunal, and I have thought about that mostly during these three and a half years, since I've been here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We showed a tape here, some footage of JNA soldiers being brought out of the Vukovar Hospital who had previously been captured there, and in this footage you recognised Major Tesic and then officers from the LADPVO you recognised, and you explained to the Chamber that you cannot be seen in the footage. When my learned friend from the Prosecution showed you a part of your testimony before the military tribunal, he said that you stated that it was your assignment to bring the soldiers out of the hospital. So my question is: This footage, which has been tendered into evidence as proposed by us, what does it confirm? Since you cannot see on it that you are bringing out the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would respond like this: Then and now, I considered myself to be a member of the unit of the Guards Motorised Brigade. If I was ever imprecise, I was not imprecise with the intent to deceive anyone or to give any misinformation. If I say that it was my assignment to bring someone out, at the time it seemed logical to me. I didn't want to misinform anyone or lead anyone to the wrong conclusion. But specifically, I did not participate in the actual act of bringing out Corporal Jovic and the other -- Sergeant Jovic and the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This exhibit, 787, is actually evidence where you indicate that your statements in 1998 were imprecise, so the obvious example of that is this footage showing where the soldiers were being brought out.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is something up to the Judges to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what is your view?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I, as a person, I, myself, Miroslav Radic, did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The Prosecutor showed you the statement by Dr. Njavro when he said that you and reservist Kuzmic went around the hospital and were checking up, seeing who the patients were. The statement by Witness P012, on page 3727, stated that, with Kuzmic, there was Sasa Bojkovski, and that he knew him because he saw him in the film "100 Days of Vukovar" when he stated his famous sentence, "Vukovar must fall tonight." So my question is: Did you see that film?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw it a long time before I actually came to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the 19th of November you briefly entered the hospital, and that Tesic and Bojkovski were already inside and also another person whose name you know now, the name of Reserve Officer Kuzmic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were another two soldiers there, but I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When, on the 19th of November, you went to check on the security of the hospital which was held by your soldiers, when you went to check on the external security of the hospital, did Sasa Bojkovski stay inside with Tesic and Kuzmic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that because I wasn't really paying attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Did he go out with you or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall anybody going outside with me. All I know is that when I went outside, I then did not return to the hospital ever again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness P030 said that on the 20th of November, you took part in the evacuation; more precisely, that you assisted in the search of those captured. And then on the same day, in the barracks, you took out 15 soldiers from the list and returned to the hospital. You denied that in response to a question that I put to you. So now I would like to ask you again: On the 20th of November, what sort of uniform were you wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state that on the 19th, in the evening, I received a new camouflage uniform from the company officer that I changed - I was happy to be clean after a long time - and that I did not take this uniform off until I arrived in Belgrade -- when we came to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what did this uniform look like? Can you give us more details?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a camouflage uniform with a pattern worn by some of the units at the time. I think these were military police units. So it was the camouflage pattern in a light green, dark green and brown combination of colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you wear a beret, a red beret?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Guards Brigade and I never had a beret, although that unit, after I left the army, did wear such berets. But I never placed a beret like that on my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question referred to Vukovar. On the 20th of November, were you wearing a red beret on your head?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: That day, at any point in time, at the hospital or at the barracks, did you wear a leather jacket?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't even go to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This witness claims that the person who took part in the actions was up to 40 years old and that they were between 185 and -- 175 and 180 centimetres tall. How tall are you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am 1 metre, 91.5 centimetres tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now look at Exhibit 430 on the monitors, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can just run over this quickly. I've just seen it now. Maybe we can look at Exhibit 410 first. It's an order from the commander of OG South dated the 29th of October 1991. Thank you. Could you please zoom in on paragraph 2, item 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, since witnesses of the Prosecution and expert witnesses and other witnesses read this document, you don't need to read it now. But from this order, it's evident that under item 2, "Tasks to the Units," paragraph 1, "Composition of Assault Detachment 1," could you please kindly read what the composition was of the assault detachment on the 29th of October?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2, paragraph 1 -- paragraph 2, item 1, it says: [As read] "Composition of Assault Detachment 1: 1st Motorised Battalion; 1st Platoon of the 3rd Company of the 2nd Military Police Battalion; Leva Supoderica Detachment; Petrova Gora Detachment; Volunteers Company from Novi Sad; 1 M84 tank. 1st platoon of the 1st Company, 1st platoon of the 1st Pioneer's Company, a part of the TO unit from the current sector are to extend the attack and, in coordinated action with Detachment 2 --"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Later they will describe the axis, but my question is: It was the first time that the Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora detachments became part of the 1st Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This assignment issued by the commander of OG South, Colonel Mrksic, assigns the subordinate units to their tasks, determines the composition of these subordinate units, specifically of Assault Detachment 1, and defines their assignments. From what I could see, based on the documents that were available to me and from the documents I saw, this is the first time that the Leva Supoderica detachment and the TO Petrova Gora detachment were subordinated to the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the tasks and commands to the Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora detachments were issued by Borivoje Tesic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Mrksic ordered it to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now look at Exhibit 430.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I just would like to say that this is my understanding of this order, because I did not see this order or any order in their written form in Vukovar. But this is how I understand them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can see on the monitor the decision of the 14th of November, 1991, of the commander of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Two or three things. First, we didn't go into the last document; we haven't gone into this document here during cross-examination. This is just examination-in-chief being done. This is whatever they didn't do previously, they are trying to do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, surely you have challenged the evidence of this witness as to the composition of the assault detachment after the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But not on the documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you've raised the issue. This is the way the Defence is dealing with the issue you have raised. That's perfectly proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The other objection I have is if he could be a little less leading on these issues so I don't have to get up and object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Borovic, but a little less leading is asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please zoom in on item 2, "Assignments to Units," and then go to the paragraph marked "4"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you kindly read this paragraph under number 4.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Assault Detachment 1, without the 1st Motorised Battalion, from the current combat disposition sector is to be transferred to the axis Dalmatinska street, Alija Alagica street and the water tower, with the assignment."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Who is now in command of Assault Detachment 1?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the first to the last moment, the assault detachment was under the command of Major Borivoje Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we say "without the 1st Motorised Battalion," what does that mean? What was the composition of Assault Detachment 1 then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this order, issued by Colonel Mrksic to the commanders of all subordinate units, the Assault Detachment 1 comprises, as we read in the previous decision of the OG South commander, without the 1st Motorised Battalion. So all the companies and batteries of 120-millimetre mortars are taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the axis of Assault Detachment 1. Is that an axis that has nothing to do with the axis of your third company?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that I was never in Dalmatinska street or in the street of Alija Alagica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please be so kind as to read out paragraph 5 now, which has to do with the tasks of the 1st Motorised Battalion that was taken out of the 1st Assault Detachment, the so-called JOD 1?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 5, the commander of the Operations Group is issuing a separate task for the 1st Motorised Battalion, and he says: "The 1st Motorised Battalion, from the current sector of the combat disposition, should secure the line achieved, establish full control of the area taken, and act in concert with the forces that are attacking along the following axis: Sundaciceva street; Marsala Tita street. Stand ready to take active action along the axis of Milovo Brdo, the bridges on the Vuka River."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, the commander of the Operations Group South spelled out in concrete terms the task of the commander of JOD 1, and through his own order, he told him that the 1st Motorised Battalion, which is a unit based on establishment, should remain in the sector where they were, where they got to during combat action; and that they should establish full control there and that they should act in concert with the forces that were attacking. And those forces were the other forces from the assault detachment that we referred to a few minutes ago and that were moving along the mentioned axis. And it says: "Stand ready to take active action"; that is to say, if there is a counterattack by the opposing side, they were duty-bound to accept --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak a little slower. Perhaps not everything is in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, the forces of the 1st Motorised Battalion, in case of a possible counterattack, were duty-bound to engage in battle so as to facilitate the attack of the forces that were attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I understand this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about Major Borivoje Tesic, who was then, at the same time, the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion and the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment that is now on a completely different axis of action compared to your own?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a decision of Colonel Mrksic, the commander of the operative group, not my decision. He is responsible for the 1st Motorised Battalion and for JOD 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So who is issuing commands, who is issuing assignments, tasks, after this period all the way up to the fall of Vukovar, as far as the Territorial Defence and Leva Supoderica is concerned? Is it Major Tesic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way in which Major Tesic regulated this, with the units that were subordinated to him at that point in time, is something that I don't know. I really do not want to say anything that I did not see myself or participate in myself. Now, what it was that he ordered to JOD, or rather to Leva Supoderica, and what was it that he ordered to the Territorial Defence, that is something that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that he was the commander of those units at the time because they were within JOD 1; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. It's very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're getting too eager, Mr. Borovic. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: After all, the documents are self-explanatory, so you don't even have to answer, Mr. Radic. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to answer in the following way: From the moment when we got out to Milovo Brdo, every day Major Tesic was in that sector, which is to say that that was not the case until they reached Milovo Brdo. I assume that from that moment, Major Tesic took over control over future developments. He can confirm that or he can deny that. That is my opinion. Now, how he did that is something that he knows best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You are doing your best to be fair to Major Tesic, which is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we see Exhibit 431 on the screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It is a decision dated the 16th of November, 1991, and in paragraph 2, tasks issued to units, it says, under number 1, that: "The 1st Motorised Battalion, in accordance with the assignment of the 14th of November --" sorry "- in accordance with the assignment of the 14th of November, 1991, with the support of part of the forces of the armoured battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade, should continue its attack ..." and so on and so forth. My question is as follows: At this point in time, under whose command were the Territorial Defence detachments and the Leva Supoderica detachment, after the 16th of November?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the order of the 14th of November did not change, according to my understanding, they were still under the control of Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
