utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: After the liberation or fall of Vukovar, depending on the interpretation of the parties in these proceedings, in your view, did the need cease for the existence of the 1st Assault Detachment, JOD 1, as well as the other assault detachments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual state of affairs was that the decision on the existence of assault detachments is made by the superior officer; in this case it was Colonel Mrksic. If he decides that there is no reason, then he is going to disband them. If he decides that there is a reason for that, then they will go on existing. So it is not for me to assess whether it's necessary or not. I can assess what is going on in my own domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you stated that they were of a temporary nature until the mission was accomplished, the assault groups and the assault detachments that is, once combat ceases, what is your understanding, irrespective of the commander's decision? Is there no longer a military necessity for the existence of these groups?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I was a soldier, and as an a soldier I'm giving you an answer. The superior officer is the one who decides on that necessity. Therefore, it is only Colonel Mrksic who was in charge and who would say whether they would exist or would not exist. Whether he did that or not is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. My colleague, Mr. Weiner, quoted part of the statement made by Witness Ljubisa Vukasinovic. On the basis of that, I give myself the right, or rather I also say that Ljubisa Vukasinovic, in that statement, said that he, on the 20th, was the person who searched and took away people from the hospital to the bus, and also that he was the person who returned 15 people from the barracks to the Vukovar Hospital on orders. Are you aware of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that I did not do that. What I read on that piece of paper -- well, Mr. Vukasinovic will have the right to confirm or deny that. But I'm saying that I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, my learned friend, Mr. Weiner, asked you why you did not ask for Borivoje Tesic to be called to give evidence before this Court, and you said that he would have been a Prosecution witness so why didn't they do it. My question is: Do you know that Borivoje Tesic was on the witness list of the first accused, Mrksic? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is that one of the reasons why you did not insist that we put him on our witness list? Just a moment, please, before you answer. Was that one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to go into those reasons. Mr. Borivoje Tesic, in my view, was not a witness that I was supposed to call for my own defence. I have the right to defend myself as I believe is best for me. If somebody thought that they were supposed to bring him here, I was absolutely not opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not opposed to that at all. But did you think that Slavko Stijakovic, the deputy commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, was a perfectly adequate replacement who could explain to this Trial Chamber and the Prosecution your tasks and your position in the chain of command and control?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is not a position that can be taken in the way of evidence from this witness. You're really just trying to justify your own decisions, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. Thank you. Since Mr. Weiner quoted Tesic on several occasions, I would like to ask for the English version to be placed on the ELMO, that is to say, of Borivoje Tesic's statement of October 2003, paragraph 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, this is a statement that Tesic gave to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, and we are just going to refer to one particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, there is a technical problem which may be able to be corrected shortly, but in the meantime, is this document on e-court? If it is, we could bring it up on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it will be simpler, since only one single sentence is being put to the witness, that we give the Prosecutor this English version, that I read the B/C/S version and that I put it to the witness. It will go very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you take the English version from Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we do not have any documents, so could we please receive a copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The interpreters are indicating they haven't anything. Mr. Weiner is happy now but not the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have my own copy. The interpreters can take the additional copy, if they would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we get the additional copy to the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is just one sentence. It's not a problem. I'm going to read it and this will make it easy for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Radic, Mr. Weiner claimed that you invented this dinner with the commander of the mortar company, Vuckovic, and he compared that dinner with some dinners where people from some other cases were invited. You told the Court here that on the 20th, in the evening, after the briefing, you went to the commander of the mortar company, Vuckovic, and you described who was there. Tesic, in this statement of his that he gave to the OTP, says the following in paragraph 48: "The commander of my mortar company later told me that Radic stayed with him on the 20th of November, 1991, up to late at night." Does that correspond to what you stated to the OTP, that until late at night, you stayed at the dinner hosted by Vuckovic, commander of the mortar unit? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I agree, but I can just repeat that that night I was in the house where Lieutenant Vuckovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree; yes or no? I mean with what Borivoje Tesic stated. Is that it or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the Prosecutor told you that you never stated before that your people had committed a crime and that you did not deny that anywhere, you challenged all the counts of the indictment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is there a count in the indictment that refers to your responsibility for crimes committed by your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you challenge that as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Jaksic, at this trial, as commander of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar, said, verbatim: "I issued orders to my own company commanders of the Territorial Defence, and the commanders of the companies of the JNA were receiving direct orders from Major Tesic." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Major Tesic issued assignments to me and to the other company commanders when I was present. Now, who he issued tasks to as well when I was not present, that is something I don't know about. Now, whether Mr. Jaksic issued assignments to his own lower-ranking commanders, I don't know. I did not see that with my own eyes, but I have no reason to doubt anything. And I find what he said before this Trial Chamber to be quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And finally, my learned friend referred to what Witness P024 stated, talking about the subordination of his unit commander to you. Do you know that in this courtroom we produced Exhibit 198, that is to say, a photograph on which we see Seselj; Tesic; Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni; and that precisely this witness, P024, that the Prosecutor asked you about, did not recognise his own commander Lancuzanin? Rather, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of all that you heard, do you still maintain what you said to the Prosecution, that this witness fabricated a lot here at this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You're asking him to comment upon the credibility of a witness as a direct question. That's for the Court, not for this witness to determine, credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, I think that this is the time for me to complete my redirect -- I'm sorry, yes, my redirect. And since I have now concluded my examination, and I did not take a lot of your time, I think that this is now the last opportunity for the witness to address the Court, if he thinks he has anything to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything further, Mr. Radic, you wish to add to your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you to give me this opportunity to address you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Procedurally, Mr. Borovic, this is out of order. If there was some matter that was still concerning Mr. Radic about his evidence, we would certainly be prepared to hear it right now. But a full statement of some sort from Mr. Radic at this point is not something that should occur. It should have been part of his evidence-in-chief and, therefore, subject to cross-examination. So I'm afraid, Mr. Radic, I would confine you to the issue of whether there is something you feel needs to be added to what you said in evidence that hasn't been made clear. If there is anything of that nature, mention it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish to say the following: The Yugoslav People's Army is an army in which I served for eight full years. In those eight years, I strived to be an honourable officer. The gentleman from the Prosecution has put it to me that I was derelict in the performance of my duties. I cannot accept this view of the Prosecution. At the time when I was told -- and in fact when I myself stated that the first time that I heard, or rather read in a paper in 1992, sometime in mid-1992, that something like that happened at all, and I was not given an opportunity to state why I did not believe in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although the Trial Chamber is very patient, I would not like to abuse their patience. So please be very, very brief and mention only items that have already been mentioned by Mr. Weiner in his cross-examination and do not go beyond that. I am duty-bound to make this instruction because I have to follow the procedure, and I'm afraid that you are going to go into too many details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first article that I read about me in Vukovar was entitled, "100 Days of Hell for Captain Radic in Vukovar." At that time I had been in Vukovar for only 20 days. This is one of the reasons why I was not convinced that the article, which was also available to me at the time, that it was truthful. That article presented some situations that definitely had not happened. And I would like the Court to use its authority to locate this article - I think it was published either in April or May 1992 - because Mr. Weiner put it to me that I invented this article, and this is not so. So if you could please check this, I would really like to ask you to do so. A little while ago, there was a report in the media that Witness P013 stated that I had raped and then killed a woman, and this is not something that we heard from this witness before this Court, because this is something that it was -- this is simply something that was not true. So I simply do not trust reporters, and that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I've concluded my re-examination, and we have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Thank you, Mr. Radic. That concludes your evidence. You may now return to your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you ready with your next witness, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm ready, but I completely lost track of time. Okay. So if we work until a quarter to 1, then we can proceed with our next witness. I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We rise at a quarter to 1.00, and we resume again at 2.00 until about quarter to 4.00. Today we must stop then because of commitments by the Chamber, but tomorrow we will be sitting through to 5.00 again. So we are trying to catch up some of the time that you, unfortunately, lost. You'll manage, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for your support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we begin, Your Honours, I would like to hand over the documents to this witness. These are the orders that we've seen on the screen, the combat log of the 1st Motorised -- of the Guards Motorised Brigade, so that the witness is able to use them if he wishes to do so. But everything will also be on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are there copies for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is all in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're planning that the witness will have the B/C/S and the Chamber will have English on the screen; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. We will try and bring up the individual English versions on our screens so that the accused can have the B/C/S version on their screens. I would mention that I've noticed that there are only two monitors for the accused at the moment. We will ensure that, as soon as practical, the third monitor is installed in this courtroom. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it would be more practical for us to lose one of the accused in the dock, but it's just a joke. Then we would have enough room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stijakovic, please be so kind and say something about yourself; when you were born, where you were born. And what is your family situation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Slavko Stijakovic. I was born on the 12th of July, 1960, in Banja Luka. There were four children in my family. My parents were workers; they worked in a factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us something about your education. In fact, what schools have you graduated from before enrolling in the military academy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I enrolled in the military academy, I graduated -- I first attended elementary school in my hometown, Banja Luka, and then I went to the secondary military school in Sarajevo. And after I graduated from the secondary military school, I served for two years as a non-commissioned officer in a garrison in Bar, which is a town in Montenegro. And as one of the best non-commissioned officers in that unit, I was then sent to study at the military academy of the ground forces in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, after you graduated from the military academy, could you please describe where you served, in what army, in what units, all the way up to the end. So that I don't keep interrupting you with questions, I think you can just give us a brief list.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: When I was still a non-commissioned officer, upon my graduation from the secondary military school, I enrolled in the faculty of political science, and when I enrolled in the military academy, the knowledge that I gained made it possible for me to be quite a successful student in the military academy, so that I had an average mark of 4 -- of 945, at the academy. Because I was a good student, a very good student, I remained in Sarajevo, in the ground forces training centre, where I was the commander of the unit of new students, and I also taught tactics as a subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did your military career proceed from there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was a good teacher, after two years of serving in the Sarajevo garrison, my superior officers proposed me to be promoted to the rank of captain. When I received the rank of captain, and in light of my rank and the assessments that I received, that I was given, the evaluation, it was the usual practice in the JNA for such officers to be appointed to responsible posts in the best units, in the elite units of the Yugoslav People's Army. And so, in 1989, based on the proposal of my superior officers from the training centre in Sarajevo, I was transferred to the Guards Motorised Brigade in Belgrade where I was the commander of the company that was securing Dvorovi. These were -- this was a special facility that was secured by this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Until your arrival in Vukovar, which duties did you perform?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of the company that provided security for Dvorovi, but in light of my military knowledge that I gained during my education, my superior command, headed by the commander, Colonel Mile Mrksic, proposed me to take a higher post. That would be the deputy commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, where I served as the deputy of the commander, Major Borivoje Tesic. And I was holding that post when the events of 1990 and 1991 began to unfold, the beginning of this unfortunate war in the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you were in the Guards Motorised Brigade. We heard some opinions, and the Defence and the Prosecution have an idea what kind of a unit it is. As an officer of the Guards Motorised Brigade, what can you tell us? What was the composition of this unit, in military terms? What was the ethnic composition of its troops? And what were the soldiers and the officers like in the Guards Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was a unit that choice personnel was assigned to, and many elements were taken into account in the process of selection. But the key factor that decided whether an officer would be assigned to that unit or not was the moral qualities of the officer. In-depth checks were made for each officer before he was assigned to this unit. And I remember that when I was in the Sarajevo garrison, before I joined the Guards Brigade, I had several official interviews. And when such checks are made, of course my entire family was checked, so that it was impossible to join this unit if you -- unless you had a completely clean slate, two generations back. Your grandfather, your father, everybody in your family had to be completely clean; no criminal record, no brawls, no traffic accidents. Your family members could not have been members of any paramilitary formations in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stijakovic. We have heard here that it was an elite unit, mostly dealing with the security of high functionaries and state buildings and so on. Is that important -- is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the unit had important tasks. It secured the most important facilities and officials of the then leadership of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And was that the main assignment of the unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the main assignments of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We've heard that in different armies, especially of the western alliance, there are special units which deal with anti-terrorism and also fighting in inhabited places. You, as a Motorised Brigade, were you elite in that sense at all or in this sense that we just heard that was providing security for important officials for facilities, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can speak from the position of my own post. I was the deputy commander of the motorised Battalion. That battalion's main assignment was regular training of soldiers who would come to serve their military term of duty. After that training, the soldiers secured the special purpose facilities through guards services and duties, so their service mainly was of -- entailed classic guard duty. That would be the external perimeter of security of some facility. And - excuse me - other than that, the two battalions, the motorised battalions, had specific tasks of officially greeting and seeing off persons who came on protocol visits to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know what the task of the Guards Motorised Brigade was when it went to the Vukovar front?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The task of the Motorised Guards Brigade, when it went to the front, was the following -- I was the deputy battalion commander and I could read on the basis of the order that we received what the assignment was. There is a decision of the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade which specifies the assignment of the brigade, and I can convey what the contents of the decision are as follows: In the front sector of the town of Vukovar, unblock the blockaded barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army in the town. In the sector under the control of paramilitary rebel units of the Croatian Defence Council, unblock the captured or forcibly detained population, numbering between 5.000 to 6.000. These people were prevented from any sort of movement outside of the town itself. To secure, after that, law and order in the sector, and wait for the following assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know, when you left for this operation, the so-called Vukovar operation, what was the time period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was September 1991. It was a month when there were frequent clashes in a part of the Republic of Croatia against the Yugoslav People's Army. Some barracks were blockaded. Different information arrived through the media. Based on those events, we, as superior officers, expected that we could possibly be used, our units, in some of those focuses of crisis where conflicts were breaking out. After our unit was replenished in late September, I think this was the 30th of September, according to the regulations, we went to the broader sector of the town of Vukovar in a marching column.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you tell us, if you know, what the composition of the Guards Motorised Brigade was? And, in particular, do you know what the ethnic composition of the 1st Motorised Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: When we talking about the Guards Motorised Brigade, I know that the entire brigade went to the assignment, the entire brigade. As for the 1st Motorised Battalion, in relation to the ethnic composition issue, I can say that the composition was the same as it was in the previous years. It comprised all the national groups that were represented in our battalion. I cannot give you the percentages, but by name, by faces, through contacts with the soldiers and the officers, I know that the composition was a multi-ethnic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that it would be clear to everyone in this courtroom, could you please tell us what ethnic groups made up the entire multi-ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The officers had under them as soldiers Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Macedonians. I don't remember if there were any Slovenians. There were a few Hungarians. That was mostly the composition of the Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, where was the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion in Vukovar when these operations began? What happened at the command post? What was going on there? Who was there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the specific order of the superior command, and in terms of our assignment, we deployed the battalion to the Dubrava sector. This is an agricultural farm close to Vukovar. After a few days there, for the purposes of our assignment, we entered the town itself. Our unit was led into town by people who lived in Vukovar. It was night, and we needed some assistance to enter as easily as possible and without any problems, and to reach our march destinations. It happened that my commander, Major Tesic, myself and the entire battalion command, as we were moving on foot, somewhere in the middle of the column, we reached the beginning of the Svetozara Markovica street. Then, upon the recommendation of our guide, we met Mirko Jagetic. He is a man who lives in Vukovar. And since I'm Slavko and he's Mirko, in our use, there are some comics about Mirko and Slavko; these are well-known characters. So we met and we were joking. And he told me, "Slavko, come to my house. It's quite safe there." So that's how the command of the 1st Motorised Battalion ended up billeting in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Who was in the command of the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The command, before it set off for the front, had Major Borivoje Tesic as its commander. I was his deputy. The morale assistant was Zeljko Simanic, who, before going to the front, fell seriously ill and unfortunately he died because of this illness, so that I was then entrusted by my commander to carry out not just my regular duties but also the duties of the assistant for morale. The command also included a general desk officer, Sergeant Bojic, and also commander of the signals sector, Stamenkovic. There was also the staff command and also the signals sector. Just one moment. When we set off for our task, the superior command resubordinated a military police platoon, because that was not part of our composition to date, so that military police platoon, headed by commander second class sergeant -- lieutenant --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: -- was entrusted with providing with security for the command and to implement my assignment, because, according to the rules of service, I was the most responsible person in the command for the accommodation, security, order, discipline and all the assignments that were important to the commander, in terms of the command and the command location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The interpreters did not hear the name of the military police platoon commander, so could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Second Lieutenant Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stijakovic, can you please tell us who, and when, would come to the briefings, and what that term means at the command post?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Beside the members of the command who worked there, occasionally the briefings would be attended by subordinate officers. The term "briefing" means informing or acquainting the commander with the situation in the subordinate unit; also making proposals, what the subordinate were requesting the command to do for them; and then after that, defining the assignment by the commander to the subordinates. Most often, that was how we met and briefed each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When an assignment was issued to the subordinate, assignments -- and these would, for example, be company commanders, I assume. How many companies did you have and how many komandirs did you have?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: We had three motorised companies in the battalion. The commander of the 1st Company was Captain Bojkovski, of the second one was Captain Zirojevic, and the third company was Captain Radic. The anti-armoured one was Captain Kopcic and the deputy commander for logistics was Captain Stancic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stijakovic. You said assignments were issued. The next day, when they returned for the briefing, would they report to you on the implemented assignments, as ordered by Commander Borivoje Tesic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The method of work of our command -- the method of work of our command meant that the commander, Major Tesic, always opened the meeting. He would review the attendance. He would speak generally with the komandirs on general matters, just to sort of put a more human face on everything. After that, I would be given the floor. Then I would note and listen to all that the komandirs had to say. Like I said, the method of work implied a democratic atmosphere. Our subordinates could, at the meeting, always say everything, and I mean everything, that bothered them. They could bring up all the problems without any fear that they would be subjected to anything uncomfortable because of any weaknesses. After they would bring up whatever they had to bring up. I would most often note down what was important; I would put that in our operations and war diary. After that, most frequently, I would then have the approval from Commander Tesic to propose the use of the battalion or our unit in terms of an upcoming assignment. Then the commander would listen to the proposal, he would correct it, augment it or would just approve it. When he said, "I have decided that we are going to act in such and such a way," that would be the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was the role of the military police that you mentioned earlier? What did they do in terms of the command post? What were the tasks that you would set to them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of combat, the military police platoon would need to secure the command post with a group to prevent unauthorised access or attacks on the command post. To lose a commander or the whole command, I mean, these were very sensitive persons on the front. They also had an assignment. Since we were in a zone with a great concentration of different people - civilians; people were moving around and people lived in that area - so they needed to check, screen people, in certain places, where they were going, what they were doing. This especially applied in the area very close to the command. Also, there was the situation in the front. If it happened that our unit captured or any members of paramilitary units surrendered to them, it was their assignment that the military police would disarm those people, bind their arms, and then transport them to the place where prisoners of war were kept. This was in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that they would ever capture members of the JNA and that this would be done by some other formation that was in the same sector?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such problems. But in view of the different structure and the different problems due to a large concentration of volunteer units that happened to be there, it's possible that sometimes they also had to resolve problems of that nature, meaning that soldiers or people who were violating discipline or were obstructing the implementation of certain tasks, they needed to then bring these people under control and take them in to the superiors who would then deal with that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: One more question before the break: Did you ever hear of members of the military police, to whom you issued orders, beat up anybody who had been arrested, and that you possibly saw that? I mean, if this happened and you saw that, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of anything like that happening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Secondly, that is a very small platoon, and each section is deployed on its own task, so I doubt that they would manage to keep an eye on everything. But had I ever seen anything like that, I would definitely have that officer or soldier punished. Measures would definitely have been taken. Please, would this battalion have implemented any of its assignments if we had been beating our own soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's time for a break now, so I propose that I resume after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. We'll adjourn now and resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, could you please explain to the Court what the word "cooperation," acting in concert, "sadejstvo," means in military terms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In military terms, "sadejstvo," cooperation, acting in concert, is action through which adjacent units support each other in carrying out a specific mission or task. It can be carried out by way of fire, movement, manoeuvre, and it can also be accomplished through a mutual exchange of information during combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know which units of the Territorial Defence acted in concert with the units of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and which ones with the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the cooperating units of the Guards Motorised Brigade, I cannot remember them at this point in time because this is a higher level of command and I wasn't really interested. As for the 1st Motorised Battalion, the units that cooperated or acted in concert with them at the beginning of combat actions was the Territorial Defence detachment Petrova Gora. After a while, the Leva Supoderica Territorial Defence detachment, consisting of volunteers, on orders of the superior command, a detachment was established consisting of a territorial unit from Novi Sad. However, it actually never came to be primarily because of the personnel problems they had, notably among the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Court what axis of action of a particular unit means?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Axis of action is a line that is materialised on the ground, and it usually drawn from a point of departure and it ends with an objective; that is to say, every unit that gets an axis of action ultimately has an objective. So this line materialised on the ground means that the unit is carrying out its task on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the axis of action of Company Commander Sasa Bojkovski was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can show that on a map, if you could show me the map. I remember that that 1st Company of ours that was commanded by Captain Bojkovski was on the right flank of the battalion, and it was cooperating with the units of the 2nd Motorised Battalion. This is an axis that leads to the very centre of Vukovar, to the bridge; that is to say, from the point of departure, from the railroad, and further on through Pionirska neighbourhood and further on to the centre of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please put his question again? The interpreters could not hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: What unit of the Territorial Defence acted in concert with the unit of Sasa Bojkovski; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of combat action, along the line of use of the 1st Motorised Company, or rather on the axis where Captain Bojkovski was carrying out his task, there was a cooperating unit, and its strength was about one territorial unit of Petrova Gora, or rather territorial company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know about Stanko Vujanovic? Was he along the axis of action of the company of Captain Sasa Bojkovski?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic, a member of the territorial unit of Petrova Gora, is a person that we were familiar with from day one, from when we arrived to the theatre of war in the territory of Vukovar. In actual fact, he was in the group of guides, the people who -- before our engagement and before we entered the town itself, he came with a group of territorials to help us, that is to say, to lead every company to where it was to be used. These were people who lived there and who knew it very well. On the other hand, they had already had certain combat experience, so in this way they could also be of assistance to attain the desired objective with the smallest number of casualties possible. I remember that the first evening, when the guides came, among them there was the man called Stanko Vujanovic who led this 1st Company of ours together with Captain Bojkovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And later, did he remain on this axis of Sasa Bojkovski to act in concert with the company of Sasa Bojkovski?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's logical that the guides came from the territorial units of the Petrova Gora detachment. It is logical that a guide was from the axis where they had already carried out combat action. Also, the mentioned names, Stanko Vujanovic, the mentioned person, that is, was from a platoon or company of the Territorial Defence, which had already acted along the axis towards Pionirska neighbourhood, and it is logical that as such he was there together with Captain Bojkovski, going to the mentioned axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that they acted in concert?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Stanko Vujanovic, at the outset, had the task of a guide, until they got to the axis of use. And after that, every one of these guides returned to their original unit and continued action there. As for the 1st Company, that was a classical example of cooperation, acting in concert.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard here persons claiming that Stanko Vujanovic, with his Territorial Defence, was never on the axis of Captain Radic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already explained to you how I first saw Stanko Vujanovic and what his task was. After that, I know that the Petrova Gora detachment acted in concert with us and kept the original disposition of units; that is to say, that the mentioned person continued to act on the axis that we analysed a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of this cooperation, acting in concert, who commands units of the JNA and who commands the units of the Territorial Defence and Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As for this cooperation, acting in concert, between the Petrova Gora detachment and then after that when, in the area of responsibility, Leva Supoderica appeared as well, the actual accomplishment of the task that we had been preparing in the battalion command, and afterwards the command of the assault detachment, at that meeting and during this preparatory period for the task, what was exactly spelled out was which unit would do what, up to what point, and how. And then these units would become familiarised with this. For example, Petrova Gora, in terms of a specific task, could not have been engaged in its entirety but only according to the estimate of the commander of that unit, that part of the unit that could have carried out a particular action. I would describe this concrete task in the best way, for example, fighting for the intersection of Nova Ulica-Otokara Kersovanija. On that intersection, the cooperation went as follows: Part of our unit, in terms of its military composition, would have as a task to block a certain part of the street, specifically the right-hand side of the street. A part of Petrova Gora would block the left part of the street. The central part of the street would, say, involve a chosen group of the most courageous members of Leva Supoderica. These concrete tasks regarding a concrete facility were, in most cases, led or conducted by us active duty officers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Borovic please pause before the witness finishes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a time distance. There is a time distance, in terms of who had actual authority to command certain units. For example, specifically, our 1st Motorised Battalion, when it came to carry out its task, it was commanded by our commander, Major Borivoje Tesic. This involved the organisation of the entire unit with part of the units that were from the Guards Brigade and that were attached to us for support; the platoon of pioneers, of the MP, of the BOVs. So that is the original establishment. As for the detachment of Petrova Gora, at first it was an independent unit in the zone. Why? For several days or months - I cannot say that with any certainty now, they were carrying out certain actions in the zone where they were. So this was an organised unit which lived and waged war there until we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Who was the commander of the Territorial Defence in Vukovar; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the commander of the detachment of Petrova Gora, of the territorial composition, was Jaksic, Captain Jaksic. And who was the commander of the entire Territorial Defence in town? I don't know. I just know Captain Jaksic, commander of the detachment of Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We heard claims here that Jaksic was commander of the Territorial Defence of all of Vukovar and that he commanded all the units of the Territorial Defence in the area of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such role played by him. I just know him as the commander of the Petrova Gora detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was he at the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion when assignments were given, specific duties?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the original stage of combat actions, when these two units, that is to say, the detachment of Petrova Gora, headed by Captain Jaksic, and the 1st Motorised Battalion, headed by the commander, Major Tesic, in the original stage of the fighting, these were two parallel, in terms of their rights and responsibilities, parallel, adjacent units. As such, during this -- from time to time, my commander, with -- that is to say, Commander Tesic, with Major Jaksic, did have certain meetings and discussions as to how the units would be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know until when the commanders of the companies of the Territorial Defence came to the command post of Borivoje Tesic or of the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The commanders of companies of the Territorial Defence never came to the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion. It was only the commander of the detachment of Petrova Gora who came to the command post, the commander of the Leva Supoderica volunteer force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, since you told us that you need a map, can we see on our screens Exhibit 357. And I would ask the witness to be given a marker so that he could mark what we ask him about and what possibly the Trial Chamber will ask him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the map, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you need to have it enlarged, perhaps, so that you could see the centre better?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the built-up part of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it enlarged a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I will be able to give you my answer in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we have some technical problems today, but let's not bother them too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you can do it this way. Mr. Stijakovic, are you able to show on this map where Petrova Gora neighbourhood is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the area here. This is this area here where the crossroads is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please mark it with number 1 at the side and just circle the number itself.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Stijakovic, can you please show us where your command post was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Svetozara Markovica street. This is where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please circle it and put the number 2 next to it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, can you please show us, what was the axis of action of the 3rd Motorised Company and the axes of action of the other two companies?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please mark the axes of action of 1st Company with the Roman numeral I, the second with the Roman numeral II, and the third with the Roman numeral 3.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please mark with the number 3 the location where Milovo Brdo is, if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please circle it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 788, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will no longer need the pen for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, you mentioned assault detachments. What is an assault detachment? And do you know why and how they were established in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In my previous explanation, as for the time period in which those temporary units were formed, I wanted to get to that, but now that you've asked me this specific question, I will answer it. An assault detachment, in our doctrine, it's a temporary unit formed in order to carry out a specific task, and the specific task was defined here by engagements in a built-up area where the front is actually substantially reduced. For that reason, and in light of the fact that you had constructed areas there, built-up areas, solid walls, solid buildings, then those temporary units are formed and they have a very specific task. In light of this situation that we had on our axis of action of our battalion, the superior command, quite logically, right at the beginning of the operations, ordered that we should set up assault detachments along our axis of detachment. The 1st Assault Detachment -- there is evidence of this in the form of an order of the brigade commander. It was right at the beginning of combat. This assault detachment was composed of our three motorised companies, a tank platoon, an engineer/pioneer platoon, a platoon of armoured fighting vehicles with anti-aircraft weapons, and a military police platoon. So this was the original composition of the 1st Assault Detachment. As such, it was active up until the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened on the 29th of October, 1991, in relation to the assault detachment? And, please, we have to go a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. On the 29th of October, because of some problems that were encountered at the front, problems involving the cooperation between the battalion and the detachments of the Territorial Defence, because of certain problems that were the consequence of the fact that the defence was extremely well organised, and the actions of our opponent, the command decided to reinforce the detachment. And pursuant on the -- on an order issued on the 29th of October, the following units were added to the assault detachment: The 1st Motorised Battalion, a detachment of the Territorial Defence Petrova Gora, the Leva Supoderica volunteer detachment, and the Novi Sad Territorial Defence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like Exhibit 410 to be put on the screen, because I see that the witness has now touched upon this topic so that we don't have to get back to it. So this is the decision that the witness has just referred to, a decision dated 29 October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is item number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We've already seen this in the course of our hearing today, but please let us see it on our screens. The item number 2, "Tasks for the Units." Now I would like to ask you, Mr. Stijakovic, since you now have it in front of you, on the screen, to read this composition specified here and to tell us whether this was, in fact, the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: By way of introduction, I would like to say that, up until that date, the 1st Motorised Battalion did have a detachment but it was composed of the forces that we had brought in from Belgrade. After this order, which stipulates that "the 1st Assault Detachment will be composed of the 1st Motorised Battalion, then the military police battalion," that was already there, "the Leva Supoderica detachment, the Petrova Gora detachment, the volunteer company from Novi Sad, and one M84 tank," because in the meantime two tanks had already been destroyed, and the pioneer platoon from the 1st Pioneer Company. So that was the composition that was formed for the first time after this -- or rather, pursuant to this order. The commander of the assault detachment, quite logically, was Major Borivoje Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Because you were the deputy commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, and because you were in the area of Petrova Gora, you were able to see what the Territorial Defence had at its disposal, and my question to you is whether the Territorial Defence at Petrova Gora had its own logistics. What did it have by way of logistics in this area at the time when you arrived in the area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that the Petrova Gora detachment is a unit that was carrying out tasks there before our unit arrived. It is quite logical, then, that this unit had all the elements that were necessary for its functioning - medical service, logistics service. All aspects of logistics service were there. So, when we came there with our unit, we encountered a completely organised, self-contained composition unit that was called the Petrova Gora detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they had their medical service, their ammunition supply system, their kitchen. Did they have a fuel supply system?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the elements of logistic support were there. They were there, living there, working there, before we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA units came there, did they have their own hospital? Where did they get their ammunition from? Where did they get their meals? Was it an independent system?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA units, quite specifically the unit that I was the deputy commander of, had, for a long time, functioning lines of supply and a supply system that was functioning in peacetime, so that all the elements of logistic support simply moved to the theatre and we were able to get everything we needed from our logistics. There were some suggestions from the superior command that nothing should be taken from the locals because this area had been -- war had been going on for a long time, there was a danger of infectious diseases, and water supply could have been a problem. So we took great care to have the entire logistic support, using the lines of supply from our superior command. The logistics of our superior command was located in the village of Berak, so they either sent something to us, or some things, we went there to pick them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I would now like both of us to speak a little bit slower. When I asked you about assault groups that were called JOD 1, when you said that these were temporary forces, existing only until the completion of the task - we were talking about the assault detachment - my question is whether you know that, in this period, there were assault groups within the JOD; and what characterised them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: If we refer to the drawing that I showed you where you can quite clearly see the axis of deployment for each of our companies. When fire points would be located at one of those axes or a stronghold of the enemy, the company commander would set up an assault group. Those were temporary forces that had three to four subgroups, and their strength would be between 30 and 50 people. Those temporary forces are then organised in such a way that they simply carry out their task related to this particular objective, and after this task is completed, they go back to their original unit, platoon, company and so on. So from time to time, along our axis of action, we would set up three assault groups. Since we had three officers, it is quite clear that -- it is quite logical that they should establish such assault groups from time to time, when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that the JOD 1 was established, you also said that Major Tesic was the commander of both the Motorised Battalion and the Assault Detachment 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like Exhibit 430 to be placed on the screen. This is a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Captain Stijakovic, can you please now look at item number 4. The date of this document is the 14th of November, 1991. It is a decision. You read an order recently of the 29th of October about the composition of the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In item 4 of this decision of the 14th of November, it says that JOD 1, the 1st Assault Detachment, then in brackets, "(minus the 1st Motorised Battalion) from the current sector of combat disposition should be transferred to the axis Dalmatinska street, Alija Alagica street, water tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to read item 4, which is on next page, once we see it on our screens. No. In the same document we should see item 5. This is not it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Subitem. This is item 5 but we need subitem 5, item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At the top of page -- the next page.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Not item 2, item 4. Please, can you enlarge this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please read, Mr. Stijakovic, subitem 5.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: "The 1st Motorised Battalion, from its current sector of combat disposition, should secure the line that has been reached, establish full control of the captured territory, and effect cooperation with the forces --" I repeat: "The 1st Motorised Battalion, from the current sector of combat disposition, should secure the line that has been reached, establish full control of the captured territory, and effect cooperation with the forces attacking along the axis of Sundaciceva street-Marsala Tita street; stand ready for active action along the axis of Milovo Brdo, bridges on the Vuka River."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stijakovic, what is your interpretation, as a witness in this case, of item 4? Please now go back to item 4. You have it here in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be a problem for me to give you a graphical explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mean to draw something?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it's technically feasible, but please try to say -- okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be given a piece of paper and a pen. And can we please switch on the ELMO? And then he can make a drawing of what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, number 1, please first draw JOD 1.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of Exhibit 410?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's right, Exhibit 410. And now you can draw.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to make your letters more legible. Could you write it in block letters, in the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the Cyrillic script but I can use the Latin script, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, please use the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to put the date there, the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you now --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: A bit of an explanation, please. Please have a look at this. This is the 1st Motorised Battalion, this is the Leva Supoderica detachment, this is the Petrova Gora detachment, and this is the company of volunteers from Novi Sad. These are parallel compositions within the assault detachment, neighbours. Since Tesic was the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, and he was the top professional, of course, I assume it was only natural that he would be appointed by the command to be the commander of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the 14th.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll use the Latin script again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: 430. The 14th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: All of it remains as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Draw it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: JOD 1, and then within its composition, the following detachments: Now, Leva Supoderica, detachment Petrova Gora, the company of volunteers from Novi Sad. This is the composition of the assault detachment that was established on the 14th of November, 1991. That is -- what was the number of the item that you gave a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Item 4. So, apart from that, the 1st Motorised Battalion gets out of this composition and it becomes an independent part, and therefore the command says so in item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have this admitted into evidence, please, this sketch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 789, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, can you briefly interpret item 5 for us, where it says that "the 1st Motorised Battalion, from the current sector of the combat disposition, should secure the attained line"? On the 14th of November, what was this attained line that was being secured?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please return the sketch where I showed you the axes using units? I can tell you as well. The objective was the neighbourhood of Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: When did you go out and take Milovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Assault Detachment, according to the order of the 29th of October, on the 10th of November, 1991, got out to the feature of Milovo Brdo and, in this way, completed its action within the zone of the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the assault detachment, on which axis was it? Who commanded it, all the way up to the fall of Vukovar? And what happened to the companies that comprised the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of November, a period of regrouping of units in the zone followed. So on the 12th of November, an oral order came from the superior command that the 1st Motorised Battalion, in view of the major losses sustained, human casualties that is, and in view of the fact that it was the only one that had accomplished the task it had received, will, in a way, be resting. That is what item 5 means; to secure the attained line; that, in that zone, the leftover features should be examined; that minefields should be found; that full law and order should be established in the liberated part of town. After the order of the 14th of November, the 1st Assault Detachment, without this battalion, got the task to continue action along a new axis. This axis was Milovo Brdo, the water tower. The mentioned composition was still led and commanded by Major Borivoje Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you at Milovo Brdo on the 10th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that on the 9th, in a telephone communication, or rather I was called by the commander of our brigade, Colonel Mrksic, although this was a very rare occurrence. Knowing that this was a very important feature in terms of liberating the city, he expressed to me his hope, or rather a sentence -- question. He said, "Slavko can we get to Milovo Brdo today?" That was on the 9th of November. We could not do that. I said to him, "Comrade Colonel, we will be able to do it on the 10th." And, to our great joy, we managed to get there on the 10th. Of course, once this task was completed, it was only natural that all of those who contributed in a way to the liberation of that part of town should be present there, and I myself was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 10th of November, do you know what the 3rd Company was doing on that day, the company commanded by Radic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the 10th of November, Captain Radic, together with his company, had the most difficult task of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you -- we know that. I mean -- sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to show the territory, how big the territory was that this company had gone through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you show that on a different map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Any map. I can even --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please see 156 on our screens. Because I see that the witness is insisting. Could you just enlarge the centre, please. Just a bit more. Just a moment. Could he now please be given that pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This is a map of Vukovar. Please have a look at this map and draw what it was that you, yourself, wanted to show to the Trial Chamber now, what the route was that the 3rd Company took to Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you think it is necessary, could I please tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 790, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Company and Miroslav Radic, you said, traversed the most difficult road of all. When the task was accomplished, when they got up to Milovo Brdo, did you have any proposals, in terms of someone who had had the most difficult task of all? Did you make any proposals to Radic? Was this carried out? Could you please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Knowing what I drew a few moments ago, where the mentioned person, indeed, carried the greatest burden among all the officers who were involved in that period, at the regular briefing on the evening of the 10th, around 2000 hours, I suggested to Major Tesic that Captain Radic should be awarded for everything he had done until then, and that that award should be his departure, after more than 40 days, to go and visit his family. That would be called a "leave of award" in our army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Radic actually went to that leave as an award?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander accepted this proposal and, during the next few days, he sent Captain Radic as the first officer from these winds of war to go to Belgrade to see his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard what Captain Radic himself said about Milovo Brdo. And up to the 19th of November, when he was given the task to secure the hospital, he, with his company, his 3rd Company, did not have any task. What is your comment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the explanation given a few moments ago that I had proposed him as a candidate for an award, it was only logical that that part of the unit that had made the greatest effort of all should have a rest in the coming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have an objection. I was perhaps slightly slow to my feet and missed the start of the answer. I think my friend is leading a very important point and he's also telling the witness what Captain Radic has said and has asked him to comment on that, which, I would submit, is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic, you know the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, this is the second time that I'm doing this unintentionally. I'll put it differently, if it's not too late. I understand things when you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What were the tasks of the 3rd Motorised Company, from the 10th of November onwards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Motorised Company, as it says in the exhibit, in Exhibit 430, had the tasks of securing the attained line, establishing full control over the liberated area, and cooperate with the forces that continue the attack; that is to say, the 3rd Company most certainly could not have had any kind of combat task except for securing the attained line and maintaining what had been achieved up to then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the way it was all the way up to the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the 10th of November, until the de facto --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Excuse me again, Your Honour. I apologise for the interruption, but perhaps I'm missing something from Exhibit 430 that the witness is referring to. He was asked about the 3rd Motorised Company, being Captain Radic's company, and what they were doing in that period and he was answering that from Exhibit 430. I'm looking at the English translation of 430 and can see no reference to the 3rd Motorised Company, and it causes some concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Borovic, you could learn whether the witness is deriving this information from the exhibit or from his own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The practice is, when there is a higher level of command, like the Motorised Battalion, to get a task, the one that I read out, the practice is that it is always the lower levels of command in the most important part. I mean, that order is identically conveyed to subordinates. It is correct that I'm referring to the task of the 3rd Company which is part of the Motorised Battalion. And I'm saying that on the basis of the order that we wrote, that is to say, Major Tesic wrote, his task to the subordinate companies on the basis of this order received from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, the 3rd Company, you read out these new tasks. Up to the fall of Vukovar on the 18th of November, did it have any other tasks, or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the 18th of November, the whole battalion, not only the company, remained at Milovo Brdo, deployed according to companies from that sector. Our units did not take a single step from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was in command and who commanded the Leva Supoderica unit and the Petrova Gora Territorial Defence unit in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: From the 14th of November, in accordance with the order, Exhibit 430, the 1st Assault Detachment is still under the command of Major Borivoje Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be so kind as to put on the screen Exhibit 431.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It is an order from the Operations Group South, from the 16th of November 1991, and here we have tasks and then item 1. This is unit by unit. Mr. Stijakovic, do you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not enlarged here, but I have it in front of me. Okay. Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In item 1, what does it say in the first two lines? Because this is of interest for us in regard to this topic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: "The 1st Motorised Battalion, in accordance with the task issued on the 14th of November, 1991, with the support of a part of the forces of the armoured battalion of the Guards Brigade ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So we can see here the axis. You will explain that later. But what does it mean in accordance with the task issued on the 14th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this means that they have to cooperate with the forces along the relevant axis and stand ready in case any further order or task is issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the 16th of November, who commanded the Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora detachments?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: These detachments were commanded at all times by their commanders; Jaksic was in command of the Petrova Gora detachment, and Lancuzanin of Leva Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But was Borivoje Tesic still in command of the 1st Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Major Tesic was in command of those units and issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Vukovar on the 18th of November, these temporary combat units, the JOD 1 and the assault groups, did they cease to exist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, after combat ceased, all temporary units were disbanded. There was no need anymore for their functioning. And I remember that on the 18th, Major Borivoje Tesic, at the evening briefing, said that he was going back to his battalion and that he would not be going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what do you know about the tasks of the 3rd Motorised Company, commanded by Miroslav Radic, after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, in the evening hours, after the surrender of the paramilitary forces, all the units in the zone were tasked with increasing their vigilance because there was a possibility that some of the insurgents might try to break through or to set -- to do some diversions, engage in sabotage, and so on. Secondly, the troops would have to get organised; their strength should be established and the whereabouts of every person should be established. And every such unit had to be organised in order to be able to work and live, as necessary. A part of our unit got its next task, its order, from Major Tesic. Among them was the 3rd Motorised Company and their commander, Captain Radic. They received the task that, on the 19th of -- in the morning of the 19th, they were to continue moving across the bridge on the river Vuka, to enter the hospital compound, blockade the hospital, not allowing anyone to get out of the hospital or any persons to enter the hospital who were not authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion issued an order to Captain Radic to secure the hospital from the outside with his company, and that only his company was given this task?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I actually remember this order that was issued in the morning. It was a general rule for us in the command, in the headquarters, to have breakfast together at half past 6.00, my commander, myself, Sergeant Bojic, and whoever happened to be there.
