I remember that in the morning of the 19th, he received an order from his superior command, to personally, within an armoured personnel carrier, go to the hospital itself, get in touch with Dr. Vesna Bosanac, and to bring her safe to the superior command where there would be talks about the situation in the hospital, the evacuation of the wounded, and everything that was to follow. And Tesic communicated this order to Captain Radic, using communications equipment. We had Motorola equipment at the time. And I remember that he ordered Radic to go to the hospital and to blockade it in the way that I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: May I just add something and explain why Radic was given this task?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the city map -- perhaps we could look at the last drawing, the city map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit 156. Perhaps if we could bring this up on our screens. Can we have it enlarged so that we can see the city centre on our screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just draw two lines to explain why Radic was given this task?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be given the pen? And then he can mark on this map -- to explain on this map why Radic was given this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: This here is the hospital. This is the axis of action of Captain Radic's company up to the river Vuka, and this is his next task. So it is quite logical, and this was proper exercise of command, for the commander to use the company that is already on this axis. And it is quite logical that the commander ordered Captain Bojkovski and his company to go to the city centre itself and it is quite logical that he ordered Captain Zirojevic to go to the Dunav hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark this axis with number 1, Zirojevic's axis with number 2, and Bojkovski's axis with number 3.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to admit this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 791, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, on the 19th of November, were you in the hospital area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please give us some more details about who was there at the hospital, whether Captain Radic's company was, indeed, securing the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that Major Tesic had been given a specific task to establish contact with Dr. Vesna Bosanac and to transport her --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if I could interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lunny?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The witness was asked if he was in the hospital on the 19th of November and he said yes. There has been no notice of this whatsoever to the Prosecution, neither within the 65 ter summary, which came in two parts. There was an earlier summary in mid-July. Your Honour will recall a number of motions filed by the Prosecution for further details. Further details were provided on the 31st of July. The Prosecution was then provided with proofing notes yesterday evening, late yesterday evening, at close of business. And in none of these three documents does it ever say that this witness was at the hospital, and on that basis I would object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lunny. Your proposition may be well founded, but the evidence has relevance and we will hear it. If you're embarrassed in cross-examination about it, you can move whatever you feel is appropriate about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My learned colleague was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But because it is relevant, Mr. Stijakovic, please respond.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, in the morning, I personally, with Staff Sergeant Bojic, went to the hospital. The main reason why I went to the hospital was because I had learned that Sergeant Jovic was in the hospital. In the early days of the combat, he had gone missing, and I had an interest in this because his superior, Lieutenant-Colonel Lesanovic would often criticise or make criticism of us because we did not manage to save the young sergeant. The second reason why I went to the hospital was because I knew that Captain Radic's company was there outside of the zone. I felt a need, in light of the task that was given to Major Tesic, to be there and assist in the task that was given to Captain Radic and everybody who was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Captain Radic actually performed the task that was given by Major Tesic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived there, I think it was between 11.00 and 12.00 a.m., the hospital was quiet. There was a group of people, doctors in white coats. Soldiers were stationed around the fence, the hospital fence, in shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And was the task performed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is where Captain Radic's company really did carry out the task. Nobody came in. There were no other people. And immediately after I arrived there, which was on foot, Major Tesic arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises but we didn't get who, or what with, Major Tesic arrived.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: And when I saw that, I went back to the command post together with Staff Sergeant Bojic because I knew that he would take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who then secured the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: As I was leaving the hospital and I was on my way to the first bridge, I met Milivoje Simic, a captain whom I knew, and he was in a hurry, leading a group of his soldiers. They were police officers. And later on I learned that he relieved Radic's unit and then established full security at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Major Tesic arrived in an armoured personnel carrier, so just to have it on record. My next question: On the 19th, did you have the regular briefing at the command post, and on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In those conditions, the commander insisted on us getting together as often as possible to give him an idea of the situation, and we were supposed to give him as accurate reports as possible about our actions, as his subordinates. And on the 19th, we all gathered at around 8.00 p.m. and we had a regular briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, you said a little while ago that your task from Major Tesic, after the end of combat, was to gather all the equipment. This was a task for all the units there, in fact. Were you personally tasked with controlling or verifying the implementation of this order on the 20th, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Major Tesic was really very busy, way too busy in those days, and he knew -- in fact, he would give me some tasks of his to finish. And that is how it happened that on the 20th, in the morning, he told me that a press conference would be organised in the Dunav hotel, and since I was standing in for the non-existent assistant for morale, it was quite logical for me to go to the Dunav hotel and to check how things were going, because this was the key task in those days, one of the key tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And on the 20th of November, did you visit all the company commanders as part of your obligations as the deputy commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was general practice for all the zone to be visited, because it enabled us to control all the subordinate units, to check what they were doing. And that is why I visited all sectors of all the companies, including the Dunav hotel, in the course of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who did you encounter in the Dunav hotel that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That day, at the hotel reception of the hotel Dunav, I encountered Captain Zirojevic and Captain Radic together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you see Bojkovski that day? Because he also had part of an assignment to tour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I, again, apologise for the interruption. It strikes me, Your Honour, this borders upon an alibi for the 20th and the whereabouts of Captain Radic. There are a number of Prosecution witnesses who place Captain Radic in different places on the 20th, and I won't go into details in front of the witness. Again, this is an item that the Prosecution have had absolutely no notice of whatsoever, nor from the proofing notes, nor the two 65 ter summaries. And it strikes me this is an important matter that ought to have been intimated and, again, places the Prosecution at somewhat of a disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- do you accept as being notice at any time -- that there has been no notice of any time on the 20th when your client was at the Danube hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the summary, item 4, I just warn the Prosecution that I would ask about the 20th of November, whether he visited all three company commanders. And as part of that, I am putting this question, which is part of the summary. I don't want to interpret what the witness said, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Borovic, your client has given his evidence, as I recall it, with no mention of this. There has been no opportunity to cross-examine your client on it. The matter should not be pursued further by you, his presence at the Danube hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, although Radic said he was at the hotel Dunav, I'm going to -- well, it doesn't matter. I don't have to put this question, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I am mistaken. That is not something that I am able to recall at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to move to other questions, and then when my associates find the exact line, then -- but I do not wish to prove that you were mistaken. So let's continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It makes life easier for me if I'm not. But if I am mistaken, I'm quite happy to admit it. Carry on, Mr. Borovic, for the moment. Thank you, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, we have it. Yesterday, it was 12657, line 16. That was page 2 yesterday and page 3. But it's all right. I'm moving to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "Except that they reached the river, they had moved towards the hotel but I don't say that I had reached the hotel," are the words that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then there is also page 3, the first line from yesterday. It's there. "Hadzic and I went to the centre and stopped at the Dunav hotel," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our problem is that our pagination is different from yours. We are trying to find that reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, page 12657, line 16, and it's one of the examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is there, Mr. Borovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may clarify my own objection. It wasn't in relation to the simple attendance at the hospital. It was the further corroboration from another witness that we now have, of which no notice was given to the Prosecution. Captain Radic did say he was at the hospital yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've been distracted by the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Sorry, the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But this now borders upon alibi as opposed to Captain Radic speaking about his own movements. The fact that this hotel is, in some respects --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter that can be dealt with, if necessary, by adjournment. It's not an alibi because no offence was committed at this time. It's merely a detail of movement on a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in the end, you won out, Mr. Borovic. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since the witness -- since the witness already responded to that, I'm going to move to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a briefing on the 20th, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who was present? And were you given an assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, it was a normal attendance of all the subordinates. At the beginning of the briefing, Major Tesic, the commander, was also there. However, he knew that the next day he had to travel to Belgrade to be received by the Federal Secretary for National Defence, and he told me to conduct the briefing until its conclusion, and to receive reports of subordinated units. And then he ordered me, the next day, on the 21st, to definitely line up all the subordinate units, because on the 20th, he also came to the conclusion that the soldiers and everyone there had begun to behave a little bit more loosely. And because he was a model officer, that day he immediately suggested to have a review of the troops and to make sure that we go back to the army that we were supposed to be, that we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the briefing, which was attended by the company commanders, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the command post all the time. I remained at the command post on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 21st of November, did you carry out the assignment received from Borivoje Tesic; and if you did, would you kindly tell us how you did that, and in what way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st, and I scheduled that in the evening, since the closest assembly point was the Nova street, that was the closest point close up to the battalion, so I wanted the 1st and the 3rd companies to have a review. That was Radic. Then the next company was Zirojevic's company, and then at 10.00 would be the Bojkovic company, which was a little bit further off towards Pionirsko Naselje. At 11, it would be the anti-armour division, by Captain Kopcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, this was not completely recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, could you please do it again?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the place where we were staying and the place for review of the 3rd Motorised Company was in Nova Ulica street, the closest to the battalion command, the first review was scheduled for the 3rd Company at 0800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now remember where you carried out the review of the 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Company --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Company was assembled on the right side of Nova Ulica street, and I remember that because between the pedestrian lane and the road, there was a ditch. The company was lined up on the pedestrian lane.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where Captain Radic was billeted at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: From what I know, Captain Radic was staying at a house in Nova Ulica. That's where he was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the review of the 3rd Company, was that near the house where the captain was staying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think the house where he was staying was near the place where the review took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stijakovic. So, what was the result of that review? Were all the soldiers present? Was Captain Radic present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Radic reported to me. He submitted a report. It was the first review after a number of days. I was personally flabbergasted or astounded by the few soldiers that actually attended. Out of a total of 150 people, there were only 30 to 40 people, actually 50 people maximum, in the lineup.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where the others were from that company?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The company commander explained that. He said that the majority of the people were either wounded, killed or sick, and they had already been transported to Belgrade. But if you permit me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that review because of another detail that personally touched me. At the head of the line, there was a soldier called Zlatko Ljevar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was a soldier from my village. My village is called Motike, and it's close to Banja Luka. His two brothers went to elementary school with me. And he was a Croat. And even now, I get upset because of some things that I know from the past; namely, on the 7th of February, 1942, my village, which was populated by 60 per cent Serbs and 40 per cent of Croats, experienced an indescribable catastrophe. 3.216 Serb souls were slaughtered in one day. My grandmother survived and my father survived because the guides were Croats, and the grandfather of Zlatko Ljevar worked with my great grandfather and he didn't want to point out the house where my family, the Stijakovics, survived. So I was exceptionally pleased when I saw that Zlatko was alive. I'm sorry. I'm upset. Please excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stijakovic. Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe to the Trial Chamber the climate of command in the 1st Motorised Battalion, and what the climate was in the 3rd Company under the command of Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: The climate in a unit is not created overnight. It's a process. And this unit that we are talking about, the battalion under the command of Major Tesic, had excellent command officers. As our commander Mrksic used to say, they were like apples lined up, one next to the other. And it wasn't hard to create a good system of subordination when you had such quality officers. We knew each other well. We respected each other. And out of that mutual respect, you always had maximum discipline rise up to the surface. So, when we are talking about command and subordination in the battalion, it continued from Belgrade to Vukovar and back again. Nothing changed in that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please describe the procedure of keeping a diary that you were in charge of. And also when and how was it and where was it archived, as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: A war diary is a document that is kept in war. Our unit had such a diary that I personally kept. So, in the document, you would write down all the activities, orders, instructions, all events that were important for a certain date or that were important in order to implement a certain assignment. After combat actions were over, the return from Vukovar to Belgrade, all the documents that existed during the combat actions were submitted to the superior command for archiving or their storage, according to the law. I actually was a little bit undisciplined when this was involved, so I dictated the contents to the soldier who was with me, by the name of Dobras, certain activities from that diary which I wanted to use for my own research. So, in a way, I violated discipline when I did that. My intention was, when the circumstances were right, to prove that the soldierly/military part of the conflict between the two conflicting sides, in which I was on the winning side, would be useful in military sciences. And that is how this copy of the war diary, based on what I know, is the only document that is left, that I'm using here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell us when you submitted a copy of those notes from the diary to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I handed that over to you sometime in the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know where the first copy is, which was photocopied after that? Who did you give that to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: My copy, handwritten copy, written in blue ballpoint pen, of the original diary was written by a soldier. It's not my handwriting. This was written by the soldier Dobras. I kept it together with my other confidential documents, commendations, decorations and some other important military items. I kept that at my barracks, in my own personal strongbox, locker. After the year 2000, the Deputy Defence Minister was my acquaintance, General Ristic. He was appointed to that post. And other than you, he was the only other person who could see the contents of this handwritten copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you find out about the events at Ovcara, and when?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: I found out about the Ovcara events in 1995, when the media reported information about a number of suspects, my colleagues who were there, amongst them Captain Radic. And I found this out when I was staying in Banja Luka at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. So at the time when you were in Vukovar, you did not find out about Ovcara at all?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: One more question, even though I don't have too many questions left. We will have to finish for today, but I will put one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then for tomorrow, Your Honours, I have only a few questions left. I'm just informing my colleagues so that they can be ready about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give an interview to the Prosecution in relation to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How long was this interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: We had about an hour and a half to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And was that interview attended by any of the Defence of the accused?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And one more question on the same subject: Did you say anything there differently from what you stated here today?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: From what I know, the gentlemen from the Prosecution recorded my conversation, so this can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what did you say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO STIJAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said the same things to them as I'm saying them now. I said that I am happy to be a Defence witness. And I told you that it's not important, actually, to me in what capacity I appear before this Tribunal, whether I'm summoned to testify by you or from the other side. I am speaking the truth here, and only the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's time to finish for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we must. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of October, 2006, at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25
